documents.title: System context: what the proposal changes
documents.plain:
This dataset proposes only the scale-out design: statement lanes and tenant placement. The FFI execution layer
(FFI-01 to FFI-08) is not part of the proposal; it has landed and is drawn in `tsdb-current`.

The proposal keeps the system's people and external systems. Inside the platform's organisation boundary, statement
lanes (child processes) take over SQLite execution, the Postgres registry gains a `placement` table (tenant to node,
with leases and epochs) so any node can forward a request to the tenant's owner, and object storage later gains WAL
frames (phase two). No new external system is introduced: the forwarded hop is node-to-node inside the platform, and
the caller contract (`createClient(baseURL, appId, token)`) is unchanged. k6 and the migration and tenant CLIs are
unchanged and omitted for focus; the current dataset draws them.

**Since the source was drawn** (2026-10-12, baseline `e808983`), the FFI execution layer it marked planned has landed
on `main` (FFI-01 to FFI-08, 2026-10-14): the API process already executes SQLite through Deno FFI to the system
`libsqlite3`, classifies each statement from its plan and bounds unbounded reads with a deadline and
`sqlite3_interrupt` (HTTP 504 on expiry). Lanes, placement, forwarding and WAL shipping remain proposals; FFI plan §6
names lanes and placement as explicitly not built.

ste.text:
The proposal does not change the people or the external systems. The proposal adds three things to the platform.
Statement lanes execute the SQLite statements. A placement table in the registry shows the owner node of each tenant.
A node forwards a request to the owner node of its tenant. In phase two, object storage also keeps WAL frames.

The FFI binding is now installed on main. The API process uses it today. The lanes and the placement table are not
installed.

documents.title: Containers: one data node with statement lanes
documents.plain:
One data node of N, placement-routed. The API process keeps HTTP, auth, the reader client and the backup pipeline,
and gains a placement router, a forwarder (edges 2 and 3) and a lane supervisor (edge 4). A lane is a supervised child
process in the pattern of the reader child (`platform/ipc.ts`, `platform/layers.ts`): JSON lines over stdio, killed
and respawned by the supervisor. Lanes exist because a child process is the only unit that can be killed
mid-statement, that isolates a native crash from the API, and that has its own descriptor table. They are not the
cancellation mechanism; that is `sqlite3_interrupt` inside the lane. The hot write never waits behind reads: a
mutation takes only its own file's writer lock, and snapshots run on a read-only connection (edge 6). Placement is
the scale-out pick F: a `placement` table beside the tenant row, lease-fenced and epoch-versioned; a node that
receives a tenant it does not own answers WrongOwner and the forwarder refreshes once.

**Corrections against `main`.** (1) Source edge 7 says the API process reaches tenant files through `node:sqlite`
today. Since FFI-04 it opens them through the landed FFI binding (`platform/sqlite_ffi/`) over the system
`libsqlite3`, with the statement classifier and the deadline/interrupt path of FFI-05; the relationship is converted
as existing with that wording, and it is still retired when lanes land. (2) The source's "System libsqlite3
(planned)" box at `platform/ffi/sqlite.ts (planned)` is a shared library loaded into a process, not a container. The
binding it describes exists today at `platform/sqlite_ffi/` inside the API process; inside lanes it is planned. It is
folded into the `technology` of both containers, and its edges 5 (lane to library) and 6 (library to files) become
one planned lane-to-file relationship numbered 6. The lane's internal components are a Level 3 view, deferred to
PG-02.

ste.text:
This diagram shows one data node. The API process exists today. It receives the requests and identifies the tenant.
Today it opens the tenant files itself through the FFI binding.

In the proposal, a placement router finds the owner node of the tenant. A forwarder sends the request to the owner
node. A lane supervisor starts and stops the lanes. A lane is a child process. It executes the SQLite statements of
its tenants. The interrupt in the lane stops a long statement. The supervisor kills a lane only as the last step.

documents.title: Measured values and their limits
documents.plain:
The source diagrams quote proof-of-concept measurements from vm-1 on 2026-10-12 (language-switch study §3; raw data
in `docs/architecture/lang-switch-fable-data/` on `research/fable-lang-switch`). They are historical observations on
one host, not guarantees, and no label in this dataset carries them:

- Point read, `node:sqlite` on the main thread, p50: 8.7 to 8.9 µs.
- Point read, FFI blocking step, p50: 6.3 to 6.8 µs.
- Point read, FFI nonblocking step, p50: 44 to 69 µs; p99 240 to 2,180 µs.
- Interrupt latency, FFI nonblocking step: 0.41 ms (0.34 to 8.8 ms across runs). The study's summary rounds it to
  about 0.3 ms; the diagrams say about 0.4 ms.
- Lane kill, SIGKILL to exit: 3.8 ms; restart, spawn to first answer: 51 ms (about 55 ms in all).
- `Worker.terminate()` on a running statement: waited 24.9 s.
- File descriptors: 3 per writer handle, 2 per read-only handle (from the scale-out study, reproduced by the
  language-switch harnesses).

A bounded plan is a classification, not a timing proof: a point read does not by itself guarantee a wall-clock bound
under I/O stalls, and the blocking step cannot be interrupted. The study's own limits (§9): the FFI probe used one
connection, and the blocking pool's size and back-pressure under hundreds of long statements were not measured.

ste.text:
These values come from tests on one VM on 2026-10-12. They are not guarantees. A point read with the blocking step
took approximately 7 µs. A point read with the nonblocking step took approximately 44 to 69 µs. An interrupt stopped
a statement in approximately 0.4 ms. A lane kill and restart took approximately 55 ms. A bounded plan does not give a
time limit.

documents.title: Document DB platform: today and proposed
documents.plain:
Exists on `main`: one API process that opens every SQLite file through the FFI binding over the system `libsqlite3`
(FFI-04 replaced `node:sqlite`), the Postgres registry for tenants, keys and sessions, the DuckDB reader child, and
snapshot backups to object storage. Planned inside the same boundary: statement lanes (child processes) that execute
SQLite, a placement table so any node can forward a request to the tenant's owner, and WAL frames shipped to object
storage after the snapshot path.

ste.text:
Today, one API process opens each SQLite file through the FFI binding. The registry keeps the tenants, keys, and
sessions. The reader child keeps the event log. In the proposal, lanes execute the statements. A placement table
shows the owner node of each tenant.

documents.title: API process
documents.plain:
Exists today as the one server process (`platform/server.ts`, `platform/http/`): HTTP, authentication and tenant
context, the reader client and the backup pipeline. It already executes SQLite itself through the landed FFI layer:
the binding over the system `libsqlite3` (`platform/sqlite_ffi/`, FFI-01 to FFI-04b), the statement classifier and
the deadline-bounded nonblocking path with `sqlite3_interrupt` (FFI-05). A long statement now fails
`StatementDeadlineError` (HTTP 504) instead of blocking the event loop.

Planned: a placement router, a forwarder and a lane supervisor. Once lanes land, the API process stops touching
tenant files and sends each statement to the tenant's lane with the compiled SQL, the bind values, the deadline and
the request id.

ste.text:
The API process exists today. It receives the HTTP requests and identifies the tenant. Today it executes the SQLite
statements through the FFI binding. If a long statement passes its deadline, the API process stops it.

In the proposal, the API process does not open the tenant files. It sends each statement to a lane. It also gets a
placement router, a forwarder, and a lane supervisor.

documents.title: Statement lanes (planned)
documents.plain:
Supervised Deno child processes. Each tenant is sticky to one lane, which owns that tenant's files. A lane has a
bounded statement pool with deadlines and a per-tenant sub-cap (a tenant over its cap gets a typed QueueFull for
that tenant only), a handle LRU and read pool, a write-first scheduler and a request-id store. Each lane would load
the system `libsqlite3` with `Deno.dlopen`, one copy per lane, and use a blocking step for bounded statements and a
nonblocking step plus `sqlite3_interrupt` for the rest.

**Planned instantiation, existing code.** The binding, classifier and deadline/interrupt path a lane would run
already exist in the API process (`platform/sqlite_ffi/`), written so they move into a lane without change (FFI plan
§6). The lane process, its scheduler, statement pool, handle pool, request-id store and the supervisor do not exist.
The lane's internal components are on the lane component view, and its four key flows are dynamic views linked from
the container and component views.

ste.text:
A lane is a child process of the API process. It is not installed. Each tenant goes to one lane. The lane executes
the statements of its tenants. A pool limits the number of long statements of each tenant. The lane loads the SQLite
library through FFI. The FFI binding code exists today in the API process.

documents.title: Tenant documents
documents.plain:
One SQLite file per tenant at `TENANTS_DIR/tenantId.db`; this exists today. In the proposal only the tenant's lane
opens it: a mutation takes only its own file's writer lock (`BEGIN IMMEDIATE`), and snapshots use `VACUUM INTO` from
a read-only connection. The source box quotes descriptor costs (3 per writer handle, 2 per read-only handle); they
are measurements, listed with their provenance in "Measured values and their limits".

ste.text: Each tenant has one SQLite file. The file exists today. In the proposal, only the lane of the tenant opens the file.

documents.title: Central registry and placement
documents.plain:
The existing Postgres registry (`platform/tenants/`): tenants, hashed keys and sessions. Planned: a `placement` table
beside the tenant row with the owner node, a lease and an epoch that increases at each move. The source context draws
it as a separate software system inside the platform's organisation boundary, and this dataset follows that
abstraction; the current dataset models the same database as a container of the platform.

ste.text:
The central registry exists today. It keeps the tenants, the hashed keys, and the sessions. In the proposal, a
placement table shows the owner node of each tenant. Each row has a lease and an epoch.

documents.title: Peer data node (planned)
documents.plain:
Another data node with the same containers, which owns the tenants not placed on this node. A request for such a
tenant is forwarded over HTTP with the trusted tenant id, the placement epoch and a request id. A stale epoch answers
WrongOwner and the forwarder refreshes the placement once. A retry after a forward timeout presents the same request
id, and the owner's lane answers from its request-id store instead of running the handler again. The source draws
the peer as one box at container level; an illustrative deployment view with instances is deferred to PG-02.

ste.text:
A peer data node is a different node with the same containers. It is not installed. It owns the tenants that are not
on this node. The forwarder sends the requests for these tenants to the peer node.

documents.title: Object storage
documents.plain:
Exists today: immutable snapshots and manifests under `S3_BASE_URL` or `LOCAL_OBJECT_DIR`. Planned for phase two:
WAL frames shipped after the snapshot path.

ste.text: Object storage keeps the snapshots and the manifests today. In phase two, it also keeps WAL frames.

documents.title: Components: inside one statement lane
documents.plain:
This view proposes the inside of one statement lane: an IPC endpoint, the statement classifier, a write-first
scheduler, a bounded statement pool, a deadline watchdog, a handle LRU with a read pool, a request-id store, the FFI
binding and the logger. The lane process does not exist on `main`; the dashed boundary says so.

**What has landed since the source was drawn.** The source (2026-10-12) says nothing inside this boundary exists
except the logger. Since then FFI-01 to FFI-08 landed the FFI binding (`platform/sqlite_ffi/`), the statement
classifier (`platform/sqlite_ffi/classify.ts`) and the deadline and interrupt path, all in the API process and
written to move into a lane without change (FFI plan §6). So the classifier, the binding and the logger are
`existing` here; the watchdog, the scheduler and the handle cache are existing code with planned duties (`mixed`);
the IPC endpoint, the statement pool and the request-id store are `planned`. Element and relationship statuses
describe code and calls; the lane process that would host them is recorded once, on the dashed boundary and the
planned `Statement lanes` container (decision P3).

The classifier decides the path once per statement (edge 2). A bounded plan runs synchronously on the lane's main
thread (edges 3, 8): it cannot be interrupted. Only plans classified as bounded take this path; that classification does not
guarantee a wall-clock bound. Everything else runs
on a pool thread (edges 4, 9) and can be stopped by `sqlite3_interrupt` from the main thread (edge 11), which SQLite
documents as safe from another thread. The watchdog escalates only when an interrupt does not return (edge 12), so a
kill stays the last resort and restarts the whole lane. The scheduler keeps the item-15 guarantees per file
(`Semaphore(1)`, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`) and adds the rule that a mutation never waits on read permits. The handle cache
is today's tenant handle cache moved into the lane with a read pool beside it. The request-id store makes a
forwarded mutation idempotent: a timed-out forward is a lookup on retry, never a replay.

`libsqlite3` is a library loaded inside the lane, not a box of its own: the source's edges 13 and 14 are one
relationship, numbered 14, from the binding to the tenant documents (decision P2). Timing numbers are in "Measured
values and their limits".

ste.text:
This view shows the parts of one lane. The lane is not installed. The classifier, the FFI binding and the logger
exist today in the API process. The lane will use them without change. The watchdog, the scheduler and the handle
cache exist in part. The IPC endpoint, the statement pool and the request-id store do not exist.

The classifier selects the path of each statement. A bounded statement uses the blocking step on the main thread.
The interrupt cannot stop this step. Other statements use the nonblocking step on a pool thread. At the deadline,
the watchdog interrupts the statement. If the statement does not stop, the watchdog asks for a kill of the lane.

documents.title: Statement classifier (landed)
documents.plain:
Landed in FFI-05 as `classify(operation)` in `platform/sqlite_ffi/classify.ts`, a pure function of the operation IR
that never reads SQL text: `insert`, `patch`, `delete` and a `select` with an `_id` equality filter and no aggregate
are bounded (blocking path); every other `select`, `count` and `countBy` is unbounded (nonblocking path). This is
the source's rule ("a bounded plan, point read or single-row write, stays synchronous") in landed form.

Open point the source leaves: its statement request carries compiled SQL (edge 1), but the landed classifier needs
the operation, not SQL text. A lane therefore needs the operation or its class to travel with the statement.

ste.text:
The classifier exists today. It reads the operation, not the SQL text. An insert, a patch, a delete, and a select with an
_id equality filter and no aggregate are bounded. All other selects, and every count or countBy, are unbounded. In a lane, the request must also send the operation or its class.

documents.title: Write-first scheduler
documents.plain:
Existing today in `Storage` (`platform/sqlite.ts`, item 15): one writer connection per file under `Semaphore(1)`, at
most `WRITER_QUEUE_CAP = 1000` queued jobs, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` per mutation, and the blocking path for bounded
statements (FFI-05). Planned: the write-first rule that a mutation waits only on its own file's writer lock and
never on read permits, the hot-tenant pin, and the request-id lookup and store inside the mutation transaction.

ste.text:
The scheduler exists in part. Today one writer lock controls each file. A mutation starts with BEGIN IMMEDIATE. The
proposal adds a rule: a mutation does not wait for read permits. It also adds the request-id store.

documents.title: Bounded statement pool (planned)
documents.plain:
Planned. N permits per lane for nonblocking steps, a sub-cap per tenant, and a typed QueueFull for an over-cap
tenant only, so one tenant cannot take all the permits. Today's nearest equivalent is not per tenant: the document
reader admits at most 1000 pending queries (`QueueFullError{queue:"reader"}`) and runs at most 32 at a time
(`DOCUMENT_READ_CONCURRENCY_CAP`), for all tenants together. Nonblocking steps already run on Deno's blocking thread
pool (FFI-05); the pool and its permits are what is new.

ste.text:
The statement pool is not installed. It controls the nonblocking steps of the lane. Each tenant has a sub-cap. If a
tenant has no permit left, the pool sends a QueueFull error to that tenant only.

documents.title: Deadline watchdog
documents.plain:
Existing today (FFI-05): each unbounded statement runs under `sqlite.statementDeadlineMs`; at the deadline the
binding calls `sqlite3_interrupt` from the main thread, and `ConnectionGate` (`platform/sqlite.ts`) watches the
`statementInterruptGraceMs` grace period. A step that does not return within it poisons its connection and emits an
error-level `lifecycle` event, "statement did not return after interrupt". There is no lane to kill on `main`.

Planned: one watchdog per lane that asks the lane supervisor to kill the lane in that case (edge 12). The kill stays
the last resort.

ste.text:
The deadline and the interrupt exist today. At the deadline, the binding interrupts the statement. If the statement
does not stop in the grace period, the connection stops. In the proposal, the watchdog then asks for a kill of the
lane.

documents.title: Handle LRU and read pool
documents.plain:
Existing today: the tenant handle cache in `makeStorage` (`platform/sqlite.ts`, MT-04), 64 entries by default,
leased while in use, evicted after 60 s idle. It holds writer handles. Planned: a pool of leased read-only handles
beside it (today each document query opens and closes its own read-only connection), with a capacity derived from
the descriptor counts in "Measured values and their limits".

ste.text:
The handle cache exists today. It keeps the writer handles of the tenant files. The proposal adds a pool of read-
only handles. Today each query opens a new read-only connection.

documents.title: Request-id store (planned)
documents.plain:
Planned. A mutation stores its request id and its result inside its own transaction, so both commit together or not
at all. Before a retry runs, the lane looks the request id up: a timed-out forward becomes a lookup, never a replay.
Because the store is written in the mutation's transaction, it lives in the tenant's own SQLite file (an inference
from the source; the source does not name a table).

ste.text:
The request-id store is not installed. A mutation writes its request id and its result in the same transaction. If
the same request id comes again, the lane sends the stored result. It does not do the mutation again.

documents.title: FFI binding (landed)
documents.plain:
Landed in FFI-01 to FFI-04b as `platform/sqlite_ffi/` (the source proposed `platform/ffi/sqlite.ts`): the system
`libsqlite3` through `Deno.dlopen`, opened in serialized threading mode, with a blocking step for bounded statements
and a nonblocking step plus `sqlite3_interrupt` for the rest. It runs in the API process today and was written to
move into a lane without change. In a lane, each lane process loads its own copy of the library; `libsqlite3` is a
dependency of this component, not a container (decision P2).

ste.text:
The FFI binding exists today in the API process. It loads the system libsqlite3. It gives a blocking step, a
nonblocking step, and the interrupt. A lane will use the same binding.

documents.title: Logger / EventSink (reused)
documents.plain:
The one component the source marks as existing: the Effect logger and `EventSink` (`platform/logging/`), reused
unchanged. The planned part is where a lane writes: one JSONL directory per lane, `LOG_DIR/lane-N/date/` (the "Lane
JSONL" store), which the reader ingests like the server's.

ste.text: The logger exists today. The lane will use it without change. Each lane writes its events in its own directory.

documents.title: Flow: a point read
documents.plain:
Proposed flow from the source README ("A point read", Level 3). The API process has authenticated the request,
resolved the tenant and found it placed on this node; it sends the compiled SQL, the binds, the deadline and the
request id to the tenant's lane (1). The classifier sees a bounded plan, an indexed lookup returning at most one
row, and takes the synchronous path (2, 3). The scheduler leases a read-only handle for the tenant file (5) and runs
a blocking step on the lane's main thread (8, 14). The result goes back over IPC (1, reverse) and the handle returns
to the pool; the source gives no order between those two, so they are parallel branches.

A synchronous step cannot be interrupted, which is why only bounded plans take this path. A bounded plan is a
classification, not a timing proof. The source's timing for this step is in "Measured values and their limits".

ste.text:
The API process sends the statement to the lane. The classifier finds a bounded plan. The scheduler leases a read-
only handle. The scheduler executes a blocking step on the main thread. The lane sends the result back. The
scheduler returns the handle to the pool. The interrupt cannot stop a blocking step.

documents.title: Flow: a long query stopped at its deadline
documents.plain:
Proposed flow from the source README ("A long query with a deadline and interrupt", Level 3). The classifier sees an
unbounded plan, a list query with a user-controlled predicate or an aggregate, and takes the nonblocking path (2,
4). The pool checks the tenant's sub-cap and the lane's permits, leases a read-only handle (6) and registers the
deadline with the watchdog (10). The step runs on a pool thread through the nonblocking symbol (9, 14). At the
deadline the watchdog calls `sqlite3_interrupt(db)` from the main thread (11), the step returns `SQLITE_INTERRUPT`,
and the API process gets a typed deadline error.

The parallel group says what the README says in step 3: while the long step runs, the lane's main thread stays free
and keeps serving point reads. The two branches have no order against each other; the point read is any other
request that happens to arrive. On `main` this property already holds in the API process (FFI-05 measured a
concurrent point read finishing during a long statement).

Other outcomes are separate flows: a tenant over its sub-cap gets QueueFull (the QueueFull alternative); a step that
does not return within the grace period after the interrupt escalates to a lane kill (the kill and restart flow); a
step that finishes before its deadline simply returns its rows.

ste.text:
The classifier finds an unbounded plan. The pool leases a read-only handle and registers the deadline. The step runs
on a pool thread. The main thread continues to serve other point reads. At the deadline, the watchdog interrupts the
statement. The step stops. The lane sends a deadline error to the API process.

documents.title: Flow, alternative: refused at the tenant's cap
documents.plain:
The failure branch of the README's step 2 for long queries, drawn as its own scenario: the pool finds that the
tenant has used its whole sub-cap and refuses with a typed QueueFull for that tenant only (4, as a response). The
statement never reaches a handle or the binding, and other tenants on the same lane are not affected.

ste.text:
The pool finds that the tenant has no permit left. The pool sends a QueueFull error. The statement does not start.
Other tenants are not affected.

documents.title: Flow: a forwarded mutation (receiving node)
documents.plain:
Proposed flow from the source README ("A forwarded mutation", Level 2), on the node that receives the request. Any
node authenticates the request and derives the tenant from the credential (1, 2); the client cannot choose the
tenant. The placement says another node owns the tenant, so the forwarder sends the request to the owner with the
trusted tenant id, the placement epoch and a request id (3). The owner answers, and the result goes back to the
caller; the client contract is unchanged.

The placement router reads the owner from its cache and reads the placement table only when the cache has no entry;
that read is the same relationship 2 and is not drawn as a separate step. What the owner does is the next flow: this
logical view draws one data node, and the source's edges 4 to 6 for the owner's lane belong to the owner's own
containers. Alternatives: a stale epoch (WrongOwner) and a retry after a forward times out.

ste.text:
Any node can receive the request. The node authenticates the request and finds the tenant. The placement shows a
different owner node. The forwarder sends the request to the owner node. The request holds the tenant id, the epoch,
and a request id. The client contract does not change.

documents.title: Flow: the forwarded mutation on the owner node
documents.plain:
The second half of the README's forwarded mutation, on the owner node. The forwarded request arrived over the
receiving node's relationship 3; the logical model has no inbound edge for it, so it is not an arrow here. The owner
checks its lease and the epoch; when both are valid it sends the mutation to the tenant's lane (4). In the lane the
mutation takes only its own file's writer lock (the write-first scheduler), writes the request id and the result in
the same transaction, and commits (6; the source's 5 and 6, folded per decision P2). The result goes back to the API
process, which answers the forwarder.

ste.text:
The owner node checks its lease and the epoch. The lane locks the file of this tenant only. The lane writes the
mutation, the request id, and the result in one transaction. Then the lane commits.

documents.title: Flow, alternative: a stale epoch
documents.plain:
The failure branch of the README's step 3, drawn as its own scenario. The forward carries an epoch from the cached
placement; the node it reaches checks the epoch and answers WrongOwner because the tenant has moved. The forwarder
refreshes the placement once from the placement table (2) and forwards again with the new epoch and the same request
id (3). This scenario shows the case where the new owner is another node; when the refreshed placement names this
node, the request goes to the local lane instead (the owner-node flow).

ste.text:
The epoch in the request is old. The node answers WrongOwner. The forwarder reads the placement again one time. Then
the forwarder sends the request again with the new epoch and the same request id.

documents.title: Flow, alternative: a retry answered from the request-id store
documents.plain:
The README's step 5, drawn as its own scenario on the owner node. The first forward timed out after the owner had
committed; the forwarder retries with the same request id (4). The lane finds the request id in the request-id store
(6) and answers with the stored result instead of running the handler again. If the first attempt had not committed,
the request id is absent and the retry is an ordinary first execution (the owner-node flow). Either way the mutation
runs at most once.

ste.text:
The forward did not get an answer in time. The forwarder sends the request again with the same request id. The lane
finds the request id in the store. The lane sends the stored result. The lane does not do the mutation again.

documents.title: Flow: a lane kill and restart
documents.plain:
Proposed flow from the source README ("A lane kill and restart", Levels 2 and 3), so it shows the watchdog, a
component inside the lane, beside the lane process itself. A statement missed its deadline and its interrupt did not
return within the grace period (12). The supervisor in the API process sends SIGKILL to the lane (4). After the lane
exits, two things happen with no order between them: every statement that was in flight on that lane fails with a
typed lane-restart error, and the supervisor spawns a replacement lane with the same sticky tenant set, which then
serves the next requests for those tenants. Other lanes, the API process and the reader child are untouched.

Mutations that were in flight are resolved on retry through the request-id store, never replayed blind (README). The
source's STE text adds that the API process makes that retry with the same request id; the README does not say who
retries. Both agree the request-id store decides, which is the retry flow. Kill and restart timings are in "Measured
values and their limits".

ste.text:
The interrupt did not stop the statement. The watchdog asks the supervisor for a kill. The supervisor sends SIGKILL
to the lane. Each statement in flight on that lane fails with a lane-restart error. The supervisor spawns a new lane
for the same tenants. The other lanes continue to operate.

documents.title: Deployment: an illustrative two-node layout
documents.plain:
**Illustrative, proposed.** This view is not a claim about the actual droplet or any real host. It shows one way the
proposed containers could be placed so that the deployment semantics are visible: two data nodes, each with an API
process, two statement lanes, its tenants' files and a reader child; a registry host with the placement table; and
object storage. The number of nodes, of lanes per node and the host technology are hypothetical. Today `main` runs
one API process on one host, with no lanes and no placement (see the current dataset).

Each lane instance is an instance of the one `Statement lanes` container; each node's files are the tenants placed
on that node. Relationships between instances name the container-view relationship they instantiate. The forward
between the two API processes does not: the logical view draws the other node as one "Peer data node" box, while
here both nodes are instances of the same API process container, so the edge stands for container relationship 3
without a model link. The API process's direct file access (container relationship 7) is not drawn, because it is
retired once lanes land.

ste.text:
This deployment is an example. It does not show a real host. Each data node has an API process, two lanes, the
tenant files, and a reader process. A node forwards a request to the other node when the other node owns the tenant.

terms.definition: A customer of the platform. Each tenant has its own SQLite file.
A child process of the API process that executes the SQLite statements of its tenants.
The record of the node that owns a tenant, kept in the central registry.
A time-limited right of a node to serve a tenant.
A number in the placement row that increases at each move of the tenant.
An identifier that the lane stores with the result of a mutation.
Foreign function interface: Deno calls the C functions of the system libsqlite3.
The sqlite3_interrupt call that stops a running SQLite statement.
The time limit of one statement.
Write-ahead log: the SQLite journal. WAL frames are its units.
Send a request to the node that owns its tenant.
